look_here_first: Start with the broad, loose, cloudlike PANICLE on a basal clump. Follow individual long, spreading, flexible branches and note the small spikelets spaced apart. A mature head can detach and tumble. Purple color is only a supporting cue, not the ID; compare panicle BRANCHING and spikelet clustering with E. secundiflora.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays, Gillespie, and Kerr — specimen-backed county records in Hagenbuch & Lemke. Burnet — UT Plant Resources Center Burnet County treatment.

best_field_traits: leaf blades broader than E. lugens, often 3–7 mm wide
conspicuous tuft of hairs at top of sheath
panicle very open and broadly spreading
branches thin flexible and widely divergent
spikelets widely spaced rather than densely clumped
inflorescence often purple to reddish-purple and tumbleweed-like at maturity
morphology_keys.comparison_training: E. spectabilis is the broad airy purple one. E. secundiflora has denser clustered spikelets and ascending branches; E. lugens has much narrower involute foliage and a less flamboyant panicle.
morphology_keys.field_teaching_note: Panicle can detach as a whole at maturity; this is supportive but not unique. Kew/GrassBase gives mature spikelets often 5–7 mm long, 7–11 florets; compare intact mature material, not a field photo alone.
morphology_keys.crew_recognition_summary: BROAD OPEN TUMBLING CLOUD with individual spikelets spaced along fine spreading branches; purple is optional.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole plant with attached panicle and persistent tuft.
Entire flowerhead against contrasting background with a metric ruler.
Side-on mature panicle branch to show widely spaced separate spikelets.
Spikelet macro with calipers; sheath/collar in late-season plants.

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. secundiflora: comparatively chunky panicle, much larger many-flowered spikelets clumped along shorter ascending branches. E. intermedia and E. trichodes: also airy; sheath-throat and mature spikelet details needed. Witchgrass (Panicum capillare) may resemble a fine cloud but has different reproductive spikelet structure.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Eragrostis spectabilis — follow the real-photo field cues
steps: Find the full open PANICLE attached to a clump, rather than a loose detached panicle on the ground.
Follow the very fine flexible branches and locate individual small spikelets separated along them.
COMPARE: E. secundiflora has larger, more crowded spikelet clusters along shorter ascending branches; E. intermedia is also airy and needs sheath and spikelet confirmation.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: BROAD OPEN TUMBLING CLOUD with individual spikelets spaced along fine spreading branches; purple is optional.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Existing first flowering-clump and second panicle photos are mature/dry and visually busy; the third installed image best shows open branches but does not isolate a calibrated spikelet. Do NOT claim the violet color, collar ligule or spikelet size is arrow-verified.

items.label: 1 · Fine spread of flowering branches
items.image_role: Sparse flexible panicle branches on a green leafy tuft
items.caption: This verified local JPEG shows the fine, open flowering branches above green leaves and a basal leafy crown. Arrows point to visible coarse structures only; the roots, true ligule and measured spikelets are not resolved.
items.why_it_matters: The broad, transparent inflorescence is the first distance cue.
items.creator: David J. Stang
items.photo_status: Existing physically archived exact-source photograph: Git blob 1f2e72638e443049c56bb20a443c78e88db93f0e, 477284 decoded JPEG bytes; pixels visually checked 2026-10-23. Source Commons image by David J. Stang, CC BY-SA 4.0 verified at source page. Browser arrows identify visible panicle branches, leaf blade and partly obscured basal leafy crown, not a measured ligule or species-level microscopic anatomy. Original source identification remains provisional.

items.label: 2 · Dry mature whole flowering clump
items.image_role: Large dried clump with airy branching throughout
items.caption: This installed photograph is a mature dried specimen, not proof that flowers are purple. The clump and diffuse branches are visible.
items.why_it_matters: Recognize the overall cloud even after color fades.
items.creator: Tepeyac
items.photo_status: EXISTING CANONICAL LOCAL IMAGE. Pixel contents inspected 2026-10-20. Source-level taxon identification not independently re-vouchered. Browser arrows only to clearly visible structures; no microscopic characters inferred.

items.label: 3 · PURPLE LOVEGRASS — archived open-panicle variation
items.image_role: Source-identified open panicle photographed by Krzysztof Ziarnek; original JPEG verified archived. Specific glume, floret and ligule structures not resolved.
items.caption: Another true purple lovegrass photograph showing how loose flowering heads can overlap and vary in shape. Learn the branching architecture, but never claim individual spikelet nerves or a hair-fringed ligule from this view.
items.why_it_matters: Adds the third actual species photograph to help crews recognize varying whole-panicle appearances alongside the separate red lovegrass look-alike.
items.creator: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz
items.photo_status: PHYSICALLY ARCHIVED; pixels previously reviewed for broad organs; no microscopic arrows.

items.label: 3 · LOOK-ALIKE: red lovegrass clustered head
items.image_role: Different species: thick clusters of pink-red spikelets
items.caption: This is red lovegrass, NOT purple lovegrass. Its crowded spikelet groups visually contrast with the light cloud in the other photos.
items.why_it_matters: See how much more packed the reproductive units are.
items.creator: Linda Jo Conn
